title: Vas a triunfar  (You Are Going to Triumph)

segments.t: Cheering from the aisle, Paquita promises Mariona roles in Spain's biggest television series and marches proudly out of the theatre with Magüi. As the upbeat closing montage plays, Paquita welcomes Mariona through the door of PS Management. Listen to the finale first.
Cariño, claro que vas a triunfar.
Claro que eres una estrella.
Tú harás Velvet, Vis a vis y El secreto de Puente Viejo.
A ti ya te pillaré, Canelón. Vámonos.
Venga, desfilando.
Por favor, no me toques, señor.
¡No la toques!
Todo va genial.
A mí disimular se me da muy bien.
Si quieres, te digo que estoy muy bien.
Bienvenida.
Let's go through Paquita's triumphant exit and Mariona's welcome.
Cariño, claro que vas a triunfar.

'Darling, of course you're going to triumph.' Paquita opens with her signature term of endearment, literally "fondness", then pairs "clear that" with "you are going to triumph" to sound completely certain.
Claro que eres una estrella.
'Of course you're a star.' Repeating "clear that" hammers the encouragement home. Here Paquita uses permanent "eres" because being a star is who Mariona truly is.
Tú harás Velvet, Vis a vis y El secreto de Puente Viejo.

'You'll do Velvet, Vis a vis, and El secreto de Puente Viejo.' Instead of "going to do", Paquita steps up to the punchy one-word future "you will do" as she reels off three huge Spanish television hits of the era.
A ti ya te pillaré, Canelón. Vámonos.

'I'll catch up with you later, Canelón. Let's go.' In Spain, the casual action word "pillar" means "catch" or "nab", so "I'll catch you" promises Fernando a future reckoning. "Vámonos" glues "us" onto "we go" for a brisk "let's get out of here".
Venga, desfilando.
'Come on, marching out.' Originally used for soldiers or runway models parading in formation, this "-ando" word is a funny Spanish way to say "move along" with your head held high.
Por favor, no me toques, señor.
'Please don't touch me, sir.' Swapping "her" for "me" turns Magüi's earlier warning into "don't touch me". Adding polite "señor" at the end makes Paquita's brush-off extra icy.
¡No la toques!
'Don't touch her!' Backing her boss up on cue, Magüi fires the exact same three-word warning back at the staff member, swapping "me" back to "la" for Paquita.
Todo va genial.

'Everything is going great.' Literally, "all goes brilliant", using "goes" just like English "how's it going?". In Spain, "genial" is a favourite everyday praise word meaning "great" or "brilliant", rather than "friendly".
A mí disimular se me da muy bien.

'Putting on a brave face comes very naturally to me.' The basic word "disimular" means hiding your real feelings and acting as if nothing happened. Around it, "it gives itself very well to me" is Spain's go-to idiom for being naturally good at any skill.
Si quieres, te digo que estoy muy bien.

'If you like, I'll tell you I'm doing really well.' Notice unaccented "si" for "if", versus accented "sí" for "yes", followed by "you want" where English says "if you like". Present-tense "I tell you" naturally covers an immediate offer.
Bienvenida.

'Welcome.' Built from "well" and "arrived", Spanish "welcome" changes its ending to match whoever walks through the door. Ending in "-a" greets Mariona personally as the newest actress at PS Management. Now let's listen to the whole scene again.
Cariño, claro que vas a triunfar.
Claro que eres una estrella.
Tú harás Velvet, Vis a vis y El secreto de Puente Viejo.
A ti ya te pillaré, Canelón. Vámonos.
Venga, desfilando.
Por favor, no me toques, señor.
¡No la toques!
Todo va genial.
A mí disimular se me da muy bien.
Si quieres, te digo que estoy muy bien.
Bienvenida.
You heard how Spanish cheers a future star on, marches out in style, talks about being good at something, and says "welcome". See you next time.
¡Nos vemos!
